# How empirical research on green bonds can be systematically categorized according to their primary research objectives

Empirical research on green bonds is best understood as a field that is not neatly partitioned into one objective category per paper, but rather organized around a small number of **overlapping primary objectives**. The literature most commonly treats these categories as **mutually reinforcing** rather than mutually exclusive: studies often ask about **market outcomes**, **environmental impact**, **certification and credibility**, and **greenwashing or credibility gaps** at the same time [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-F4][N5-R1][N6-R2][N7-R2]. This overlap means that any systematic categorization must recognize that the same paper can belong to more than one objective category, and that these categories are not cleanly separable in empirical design [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R1][N6-R2][N7-R2].

## 1) The main objective categories used in the literature

The empirical literature on green bonds is organized around five main objective categories, with the first four being especially dominant:

### 1.1) **Market and pricing outcomes**
This is one of the most common categories. The literature frequently asks how green bonds are priced, whether they show a “green premium,” and how market participants react to them. Studies in this category examine yield spreads, pricing efficiency, investor sentiment, and market contagion, often comparing green bonds with conventional bonds [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. These studies are often framed as market-based investigations of how investors and traders interpret green bonds, and they are especially common in papers on green bond pricing anomalies and investor behavior [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

### 1.2) **Environmental impact and effectiveness**
A second major category is whether green bonds actually improve environmental outcomes. This includes studies of carbon reduction, emissions intensity, ecological footprint, and broader sustainability performance [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. Some papers also examine whether green bond issuance is associated with improved corporate environmental performance, often with a focus on emissions, pollution control, or other environmental metrics [N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. This category is often the environmental counterpart to the market category: it asks whether the bond delivers real environmental benefits, not just whether investors think it does [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

### 1.3) **Certification and credibility**
A growing but still narrower category is the study of certification, disclosure, and verification. Papers in this category examine how third-party certification affects pricing, market trust, and perceived credibility [N3-F3][N4-F4]. They often ask whether certification actually improves outcomes or whether it merely signals credibility without affecting the real environmental effect [N3-F3][N4-F4]. These studies are especially relevant because certification is central to how investors interpret green bonds, and because verification is increasingly treated as a market prerequisite rather than an optional feature [N4-F4][N4-R4].

### 1.4) **Greenwashing, verification gaps, and credibility mechanisms**
This category is closely related to certification and credibility but is often framed as a **structural limitation** rather than merely a descriptive topic. It asks whether green bonds are genuinely green, whether they reflect opportunistic signaling, and whether verification gaps or credibility gaps exist in the market [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3]. Some studies argue that greenwashing is not widespread but that credibility gaps remain important concerns [N7-R2]. This category is especially important because it addresses the **quality of evidence** underlying the other categories: if certification is weak, the environmental and market effects may be overstated [N3-F3][N4-F4][N7-R2].

### 1.5) **Policy and regulatory design**
While less explicitly emphasized in the provided evidence than the other categories, policy questions are still present in the literature. They arise especially in studies of certification, disclosure, verification, and regional standards, because these mechanisms shape whether green bonds can be trusted and how they are governed [N1-F1][N4-F4][N7-R2]. The evidence also suggests that regional and standard-based frameworks vary, which implies that policy design is an important underlying concern for empirical research [N1-F1][N4-F4].

## 2) Why the same study can belong to more than one category

A major reason the literature is not cleanly divided into a single category per paper is that **research questions often overlap**. For example:

- A paper on whether green bonds improve environmental performance may also be concerned with certification quality, because third-party certification is central to whether the environmental effect is credible [N3-F3][N4-F4].
- A study on investor sentiment or pricing may also touch on disclosure quality or credibility, because investor behavior depends on how investors interpret the greenness and reliability of the bond [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N4-F4].
- A study on greenwashing may also be framed as an issue of market outcomes or investor behavior, because credibility gaps affect how investors price and trade green bonds [N7-R1][N7-R3][N5-R1].

In short, the literature often treats **policy, market, and environmental questions** as interrelated rather than separate. A single empirical paper may be read as answering multiple questions at once: “Is this bond actually green?” “How is it priced?” and “Does it reduce emissions?” [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R1][N6-R2][N7-R2].

## 3) Which categories are most commonly used versus niche

The most commonly used categories are clearly **market outcomes** and **environmental impact**. The market literature is especially rich in studies of yield spreads, pricing anomalies, and investor behavior, including the green premium and pricing efficiency [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The environmental literature is also substantial, with a focus on carbon reduction, emissions intensity, and ecological outcomes [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5].

In contrast, **certification/credibility** and **greenwashing/credibility gaps** are increasingly important but still relatively narrower in scope. These categories are central to studies of third-party verification, greenwashing, and credibility mechanisms, but they are often framed as addressing gaps rather than as the dominant empirical focus [N3-F3][N4-F4][N7-R2][N7-R3]. **Policy and regulatory design** is present in the literature but thinner in the provided evidence than the other categories, especially compared to market and environmental research [N1-F1][N4-F4].

## 4) How objective framing overlaps with policy, market, and environmental questions

The overlap between objective framing and broader research questions is the defining feature of empirical green bond research. Here’s how each objective maps to a broader question domain:

### Policy questions
These are embedded in studies of certification, disclosure, verification, and regional standards. They ask whether the green bond market is trustworthy, whether verification is effective, and how different frameworks affect governance [N1-F1][N4-F4][N7-R2]. The evidence suggests that verification and certification are not merely background features; they shape the entire empirical design and interpretation [N3-F3][N4-F4].

### Market questions
These are embedded in studies of pricing, investor behavior, market efficiency, and investor sentiment. They ask how green bonds are valued and traded, and whether market participants treat them differently from conventional bonds [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. The evidence also shows that credibility mechanisms can change market outcomes directly, because investors may accept lower yields in exchange for environmental alignment [N3-F3][N5-R2].

### Environmental questions
These are embedded in studies of carbon reduction, emissions intensity, and broader ecological effects. They ask whether green bonds actually move the needle on sustainability, rather than merely signaling it [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. The evidence also shows that environmental studies often rely on firm-level or project-level data, and that verification quality is a major concern because self-reported measures may be inflated or biased [N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R5].

## 5) Systematic categorization beyond objective: classifications used in the literature

In addition to the primary objective categories, the literature uses a range of **classification schemes** to categorize green bonds. These schemes are often used to frame the research question and to compare across issuers, markets, and standards.

### 5.1) Issuance type and use-of-proceeds
The literature frequently classifies green bonds by **issuance type**, **project type**, and **use-of-proceeds**. The ICMA Green Bond Principles explicitly identify **use of proceeds** as the cornerstone of a green bond, requiring that proceeds be allocated to eligible green projects and that the legal documentation clearly describe those projects [N2-F2]. Under this scheme, common categories include standard green use-of-proceeds bonds, securitized bonds, and project bonds [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The literature also notes that green bonds can be classified by **project type**, such as renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution prevention and control, and other environmental or social projects [N2-F2]. The GBP further recognize that some green bonds may finance projects with **social objectives** or combinations of social and environmental objectives, and that this has led to related guidance for social bonds [N2-F2].

### 5.2) Certification and disclosure classifications
Certification and disclosure classifications are central to how green bonds are evaluated in the literature. The literature points to **third-party certification**, **pre-issuance disclosure**, **post-issuance reporting**, and **external verification** as key credibility mechanisms [N1-F1][N4-F4]. The Climate Bond Standard (CBS) builds on the GBP by requiring external verification and creating a certification framework [N1-F1][N4-F4]. The evidence also emphasizes that certification is not universal, that verification standards vary, and that certification is often costly and unevenly applied [N3-F3][N4-F4]. In practice, studies in this category often classify green bonds by whether they are certified, by the type of certifier, and by the intensity of disclosure requirements [N4-F4].

### 5.3) Regional and standard-based categorization
Classification schemes also vary by **jurisdiction or standard**. The literature shows that green bond frameworks vary by region and standard, with the GBP as the core international standard and regional standards built on it [N1-F1]. The evidence notes that several regional standards exist, and that they may differ in eligible green projects and external verification requirements [N1-F1]. The Climate Bonds Standard is one such regional-standard-based framework, while other standards may be country-specific or market-specific [N1-F1][N4-F4]. The literature also points to the fact that compliance with these frameworks carries additional costs, which can be challenging for small issuers and may limit the reach of a framework to a particular geographical or investor base [N1-F1].

### 5.4) How these classifications map to research questions
These classification schemes map directly to research questions:

- **Use-of-proceeds and project-type classifications** are used to ask whether the bond is actually financing the claimed environmental purpose [N2-F2].
- **Certification and disclosure classifications** are used to ask whether the bond is credible and whether investors can trust the green label [N4-F4][N7-R2][N7-R3].
- **Issuance-type classifications** are used to ask how different bond structures affect market behavior, pricing, or regulatory treatment [N2-R1][N2-R4].
- **Jurisdiction/standard-based classifications** are used to ask how regional differences in rules and verification affect issuance, certification, and investor access [N1-F1].

## 6) Empirical methods and data sources across categories

The methods and data sources used across categories are quite varied, but they tend to cluster around a few common designs.

### Market and pricing studies
These studies most commonly use regression analysis of yield spreads or pricing anomalies, often with cross-sectional or panel data on green bond issues compared to conventional bonds [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4]. They also frequently rely on bond-level data, including issuance details, maturity, coupon, rating, and market price information, and they often include proxies for investor sentiment or market conditions [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R5]. Event studies or bootstrap methods are used when the research question is about investor reaction or market contagion [N5-R1][N5-R5].

### Environmental impact studies
These studies typically use regression analysis of firm-level or project-level outcomes against green bond issuance, with dependent variables such as carbon emissions, emissions intensity, or ecological footprint [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. They often use firm-level environmental data, emissions reports, or project-level environmental metrics, and they are more likely to use panel or longitudinal designs to track changes over time [N6-R2][N6-R4][N6-R5]. Some studies also rely on firm disclosures or third-party certification status to assess whether the environmental effect is real or merely reported [N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R5].

### Certification and credibility studies
These studies commonly use regression or difference-in-differences analysis of certification status or verification intensity against pricing, reputation, or green premium outcomes [N3-F3][N4-F4]. They are often based on issuer-level data, including whether the bond is certified, the type of certifier, and the associated disclosure requirements [N4-F4].

### Greenwashing and credibility studies
These studies often combine pricing, market reaction, and certification data to infer credibility gaps [N7-R1][N7-R3]. They may use regression analysis of green bond pricing efficiency, stock market reactions, or investor sentiment against certification or verification indicators [N7-R1][N7-R3][N7-R5].

### Cross-category differences in data quality and comparability
Data quality and comparability differ substantially across categories. **Market studies** often have rich and standardized data, but **environmental studies** can be noisy, inconsistent, and difficult to measure consistently across firms or projects [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. **Certification and verification studies** depend on disclosure data, certification status, and sometimes survey or expert-based information, which can be uneven and jurisdictionally inconsistent [N3-F3][N4-F4]. **Greenwashing studies** often combine multiple data sources, which can improve robustness but also complicate comparability [N7-R1][N7-R3].

## 7) Cross-cutting issues: greenwashing, verification, and credibility

Cross-cutting issues such as **greenwashing, verification, and credibility** are central to empirical green bond research. They affect study design and interpretation in several ways.

### How verification and certification affect study design and interpretation
Verification and certification are not merely descriptive features; they shape how researchers frame the greenness of a bond, the reliability of the data, and the interpretation of market outcomes. Studies that rely on third-party certification often interpret certification as a signal of credibility, while those that do not certify may interpret the absence of certification as evidence of a credibility gap [N3-F3][N4-F4]. Studies that use external verification or assurance treat verification as a credibility-enhancing mechanism, which changes the empirical question from “is the bond green?” to “does the market treat the bond as credible?” [N4-F4][N4-R3]. This means that verification and certification are often part of the dependent variable or a key explanatory variable in empirical designs, rather than merely background information [N4-F4][N4-R3].

### Evidence on greenwashing or credibility gaps
The evidence is mixed but suggestive. On the one hand, some studies find that green bonds are associated with greenwashing, especially when certification is low or non-uniform, because firms may issue green bonds to signal environmental responsibility without substantially changing their actual practices [N3-F3][N7-R1][N7-R3]. On the other hand, the literature also notes that greenwashing is not prevalent in the green bond market, but that **ambition and credibility gaps** remain important concerns [N7-R2]. This tension implies that empirical studies must distinguish between **true greenwashing** and **perceived credibility gaps**, because the former is about intentional deception, while the latter is about market misperceptions or weak verification [N7-R1][N7-R2].

### How credibility mechanisms shape market outcomes and investor behavior
Credibility mechanisms shape market outcomes and investor behavior in several ways. First, credible certification and verification can reduce the “green premium” or make green bonds more attractive to investors with environmental missions, because investors are willing to accept lower yields in exchange for environmental alignment [N3-F3][N5-R2]. Second, credible bonds can improve pricing efficiency and investor confidence, while low credibility may raise market skepticism or reduce demand [N4-F4][N5-R1]. Third, credibility affects how investors interpret information, which in turn affects their trading behavior and sentiment contagion [N5-R1][N5-R5]. The evidence also suggests that credibility mechanisms are especially important in contexts where verification is costly or where the environmental outcome is difficult to measure, because investors rely on certification as a proxy for true greenness [N3-F3][N4-F4].

### What remains unresolved
What remains unresolved is the **quality and enforcement** of verification itself. The literature indicates that verification standards are not uniform, certification is not compulsory, and verification costs can be significant, especially for small issuers [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-F4]. This creates a gap between the existence of verification mechanisms and their actual effectiveness. The evidence also points to unresolved questions about how different verification regimes compare, how enforcement varies by jurisdiction, and whether market participants actually behave differently when verification is strong or weak [N1-F1][N4-F4][N7-R5]. In short, verification and credibility are central cross-cutting issues, but the literature is still far from consensus on whether certification actually reduces greenwashing, how verification quality varies, and how markets respond to different credibility regimes [N3-F3][N4-F4][N7-R2][N7-R5].

## 8) Bottom line: how to systematically categorize empirical green bond research

A systematic categorization of empirical green bond research can be organized as follows:

1. **Primary objectives**: market and pricing outcomes, environmental impact, certification and credibility, greenwashing and credibility gaps, and policy/regulatory design.
2. **Overlapping categories**: the same study often belongs to more than one category because market, environmental, and credibility questions are interrelated [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R1][N6-R2][N7-R2].
3. **Most common versus niche categories**: market outcomes and environmental impact are most commonly used; certification/credibility and greenwashing are increasingly important but still narrower [N5-R2][N5-R3][N6-R2][N7-R2][N7-R3].
4. **Classification schemes beyond objective**: issuance type, use-of-proceeds, project type, certification/disclosure, and regional/standard-based categorization all map to research questions and help compare across issuers, markets, and standards [N2-F2][N4-F4][N1-F1].
5. **Methods and data sources**: market studies often use yield-spread regression and investor sentiment data; environmental studies often use firm/project-level emissions data; certification studies often use issuer-level certification and disclosure data; and greenwashing studies often combine pricing, market reaction, and certification data [N5-R2][N6-R2][N3-F3][N7-R1][N7-R3].
6. **Cross-cutting issues**: greenwashing, verification, and credibility are central to study design and interpretation, but verification quality and enforcement remain unresolved [N3-F3][N4-F4][N7-R2][N7-R5].

## 9) Practical implication for systematic categorization
For researchers or reviewers, the best approach is to categorize papers along two dimensions:

- **By primary objective**: market outcomes, environmental impact, certification/credibility, greenwashing/credibility gaps, and policy/regulatory design.
- **By classification scheme**: issuance type, use-of-proceeds, project type, certification/disclosure, and jurisdiction/standard.

This dual categorization captures the main empirical directions while preserving the overlap and heterogeneity of the field [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4][N5-R1][N6-R2][N7-R2]. It also makes clear that the literature is best understood as a **multi-dimensional research space**, not a single linear taxonomy [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R1][N6-R2][N7-R2].

The same category also uses event study or bootstrap methods when the research question is about investor reaction or market contagion [N5-R1][N5-R5]. In **environmental impact studies**, the typical method is regression analysis of firm-level or project-level outcomes against green bond issuance, with dependent variables such as carbon emissions, emissions intensity, or ecological footprint [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. These studies often use firm-level data or industry-level data, and some rely on firm disclosures or third-party certification status to assess whether the environmental effect is real or merely reported [N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R5]. In **certification and credibility studies**, the common method is regression or difference-in-differences analysis of certification status or verification intensity against pricing, reputation, or green premium outcomes [N3-F3][N4-F4]. These studies are often based on issuer-level data, including whether the bond is certified, the type of certifier, and the associated disclosure requirements [N4-F4]. In **greenwashing and credibility studies**, the method is often regression analysis of green bond pricing efficiency, stock market reactions, or investor sentiment against certification or verification indicators, with a focus on whether green bonds are “genuinely” green or merely symbolic [N7-R1][N7-R3][N7-R5].

Data sources and empirical design differ across categories. **Market studies** depend heavily on secondary market data, bond-level pricing data, and investor sentiment indicators, often from exchanges or Bloomberg-style databases [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R5]. **Environmental studies** depend more on firm-level environmental data, emissions reports, or project-level environmental metrics, and they are more likely to use panel or longitudinal designs to track changes over time [N6-R2][N6-R4][N6-R5]. **Certification studies** depend on disclosure data, certification status, and sometimes survey or expert-based information on verification quality [N3-F3][N4-F4]. **Greenwashing studies** often combine pricing, market reaction, and certification data to infer credibility gaps [N7-R1][N7-R3]. The most important limitation is that data quality and comparability are uneven across categories. Market data are often rich and standardized, but environmental data can be noisy, inconsistent, and difficult to measure consistently across firms or projects [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5]. Certification and verification data are also uneven, because certification is not universal, standards vary, and verification quality depends on the certifier [N3-F3][N4-F4]. Cross-category differences are especially stark: market studies can be large and replicable, while environmental studies may suffer from weak or proprietary measurement tools; credibility studies may be small and focused on specific markets or issuers [N5-R2][N6-R2][N7-R2].

A major gap in existing research is that many studies use only **firm-level or bond-level data** rather than project-level data, making it hard to disentangle the true environmental effect of green bonds from broader firm or market effects [N6-R3][N6-R5]. Another gap is that many studies rely on **self-reported or disclosure-based measures** rather than independent verification, so their findings may be inflated or biased [N3-F3][N4-F4]. The literature also lacks consistent and comparable **certification and verification measures** across issuers, markets, and standards, which limits cross-study comparisons [N3-F3][N4-F4][N7-R2]. Finally, the evidence base is still limited on **how different verification regimes interact with market outcomes** and how enforcement quality varies by jurisdiction or standard [N4-F4][N7-R5]. Overall, the empirical methods are advancing, but the data sources remain heterogeneous and the comparability problem remains unresolved [N5-R2][N6-R2][N7-R2].

In the literature beyond objective, green bonds are classified through several distinct but interrelated schemes: **issuance type**, **project type**, **use-of-proceeds**, **certification/disclosure**, and **regional/standard-based categorization**. The most explicit and widely referenced classification is the **use-of-proceeds** scheme, which distinguishes green bonds by how their proceeds are allocated [N2-F2]. The ICMA Green Bond Principles explicitly identify **use of proceeds** as the cornerstone of a green bond, requiring that proceeds be applied to eligible green projects and that the legal documentation clearly describe those projects [N2-F2]. Under this scheme, common categories include standard green use-of-proceeds bonds, securitized bonds, and project bonds [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4]. The literature also notes that green bonds can be classified by **project type**, such as renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution prevention and control, and other environmental or social projects [N2-F2]. The GBP further recognize that some green bonds may finance projects with **social objectives** or combinations of social and environmental objectives, and that this has led to related guidance for social bonds [N2-F2].

The **issuance-type** classification is less standardized than use-of-proceeds, but still important in the literature. The evidence includes references to **use-of-proceeds bonds**, **project bonds**, **securitized bonds**, **ABS**, **MBS**, and **covered bonds** as different issuance formats [N2-R1][N2-R4]. The ICMA brochure also notes that green bonds may be used for **new and existing eligible green projects**, and that the GBP are intended to apply broadly to a variety of market participants and transaction types [N2-F2]. This suggests that issuance type is often treated as a secondary classification that interacts with project type and use-of-proceeds [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-F2].

**Certification and disclosure classifications** are central to how green bonds are evaluated in the literature. The literature points to **third-party certification**, **pre-issuance disclosure**, **post-issuance reporting**, and **external verification** as key credibility mechanisms [N1-F1][N4-F4]. The Climate Bond Standard (CBS) builds on the GBP by requiring external verification and creating a certification framework [N1-F1][N4-F4]. The evidence also emphasizes that certification is not universal, that verification standards vary, and that certification is often costly and unevenly applied [N3-F3][N4-F4]. In practice, studies in this category often classify green bonds by whether they are certified, by the type of certifier, and by the intensity of disclosure requirements [N4-F4]. These classifications map directly to research questions about credibility, greenwashing, and market trust [N4-F4][N7-R2][N7-R3].

The **jurisdiction or standard-based classification** is another important dimension. The literature shows that green bond frameworks vary by region and standard, with the GBP as the core international standard and regional standards built on it [N1-F1]. The evidence notes that several regional standards exist, and that they may differ in eligible green projects and external verification requirements [N1-F1]. The Climate Bonds Standard is one such regional-standard-based framework, while other standards may be country-specific or market-specific [N1-F1][N4-F4]. The literature also points to the fact that compliance with these frameworks carries additional costs, which can be challenging for small issuers and may limit the reach of a framework to a particular geographical or investor base [N1-F1]. This variation means that classification schemes are not universal and must be interpreted relative to the jurisdiction or standard in question [N1-F1][N4-F4].

How these classifications map to research questions is important. **Use-of-proceeds** and **project-type** classifications are used to ask whether the bond is actually financing the claimed environmental purpose [N2-F2]. **Certification and disclosure** classifications are used to ask whether the bond is credible and whether investors can trust the green label [N4-F4][N7-R2]. **Issuance-type** classifications are used to ask how different bond structures affect market behavior, pricing, or regulatory treatment [N2-R1][N2-R4]. **Jurisdiction/standard-based** classifications are used to ask how regional differences in rules and verification affect issuance, certification, and investor access [N1-F1]. In short, the literature classifies green bonds not only by what they finance, but also by how they are issued, disclosed, certified, and regulated [N2-F2][N4-F4][N1-F1].

Cross-cutting issues such as **greenwashing, verification, and credibility** are central to empirical green bond research, and they affect study design and interpretation in several ways. First, **verification and certification** are not merely descriptive features; they shape how researchers frame the greenness of a bond, the reliability of the data, and the interpretation of market outcomes. Studies that rely on third-party certification often interpret certification as a signal of credibility, while those that do not certify may interpret the absence of certification as evidence of a credibility gap [N3-F3][N4-F4]. Similarly, studies that use external verification or assurance treat verification as a credibility-enhancing mechanism, which changes the empirical question from “is the bond green?” to “does the market treat the bond as credible?” [N4-F4][N4-R3]. This means that verification and certification are often part of the dependent variable or a key explanatory variable in empirical designs, rather than merely background information [N4-F4][N4-R3].

The evidence on **greenwashing or credibility gaps** is mixed but suggestive. On the one hand, some studies find that green bonds are associated with greenwashing, especially when certification is low or non-uniform, because firms may issue green bonds to signal environmental responsibility without substantially changing their actual practices [N3-F3][N7-R1][N7-R3]. On the other hand, the literature also notes that greenwashing is not prevalent in the green bond market, but that ambition and credibility gaps remain important concerns [N7-R2]. This tension implies that empirical studies must distinguish between **true greenwashing** and **perceived credibility gaps**, because the former is about intentional deception, while the latter is about market misperceptions or weak verification [N7-R1][N7-R2]. The evidence also shows that credibility mechanisms are increasingly being treated as market prerequisites, with independent verification becoming a standard expectation rather than an optional feature [N4-F4][N4-R4].

**Credibility mechanisms** shape market outcomes and investor behavior in several ways. First, credible certification and verification reduce the “green premium” or make green bonds more attractive to investors with environmental missions, because investors are willing to accept lower yields in exchange for environmental alignment [N3-F3][N5-R2]. Second, credible bonds can improve pricing efficiency and investor confidence, while low credibility may raise market skepticism or reduce demand [N4-F4][N5-R1]. Third, credibility affects how investors interpret information, which in turn affects their trading behavior and sentiment contagion [N5-R1][N5-R5]. The evidence also suggests that credibility mechanisms are especially important in contexts where verification is costly or where the environmental outcome is difficult to measure, because investors rely on certification as a proxy for true greenness [N3-F3][N4-F4].

What remains unresolved is the **quality and enforcement** of verification itself. The literature indicates that verification standards are not uniform, certification is not compulsory, and verification costs can be significant, especially for small issuers [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-F4]. This creates a gap between the existence of verification mechanisms and their actual effectiveness. The evidence also points to unresolved questions about how different verification regimes compare, how enforcement varies by jurisdiction, and whether market participants actually behave differently when verification is strong or weak [N1-F1][N4-F4][N7-R5]. In short, verification and credibility are central cross-cutting issues, but the literature is still far from consensus on whether certification actually reduces greenwashing, how verification quality varies, and how markets respond to different credibility regimes [N3-F3][N4-F4][N7-R2][N7-R5].

Empirical green bond research is most systematically categorized around a small set of overlapping primary objectives, with the literature often treating these categories as mutually reinforcing rather than mutually exclusive. The main objective categories used in the literature are: (1) **impact and effectiveness**, especially whether green bonds improve environmental performance or emissions outcomes; (2) **market and pricing outcomes**, including yield spreads, pricing efficiency, and investor behavior; (3) **certification and credibility**, especially the role of third-party verification and how it affects perceived trustworthiness; and (4) **greenwashing, verification gaps, and credibility mechanisms**, which are increasingly framed as structural limitations rather than merely descriptive topics [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-F4][N7-R2][N7-R3].

A key pattern is that the same study can belong to more than one objective category. For example, a paper examining whether green bonds improve environmental performance may also be concerned with certification quality, because third-party certification is central to whether the environmental outcome is credible [N3-F3][N4-F4]. Similarly, a study on investor sentiment or pricing may be analyzed through market outcomes while also touching on disclosure quality or credibility, because investor behavior depends on how investors interpret the greenness and reliability of the bond [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N4-F4]. In this sense, green bond research often spans **policy, market, and environmental questions** in a single empirical design: policy questions about regulation and standards, market questions about pricing and investor behavior, and environmental questions about actual emissions or ecological outcomes [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R1][N6-R2][N7-R2].

The most commonly used categories are **market outcomes** and **environmental impact**. The market literature is especially rich in studies of yield spreads, pricing efficiency, and investor sentiment, including papers on the “green premium” and how green bond pricing differs from conventional bonds [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The environmental literature is also substantial, with a focus on carbon reduction, emissions intensity, and broader ecological effects [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. **Certification and credibility** is a growing but still somewhat niche category; it is central to studies of third-party verification and greenwashing, but these papers are often framed as addressing gaps rather than as the dominant empirical focus [N3-F3][N4-F4][N7-R2][N7-R3]. **Greenwashing** and credibility issues are especially prominent in studies that examine whether green bonds are genuinely green or whether they reflect opportunistic signaling [N7-R1][N7-R3][N7-R5]. A smaller niche is **policy and regulatory design**, though the provided evidence here is thinner on explicit policy interventions than on the empirical consequences of policy regimes [N1-F1][N4-F4].

The overlap between objective framing and broader research questions is especially clear. **Policy questions** are often embedded in studies of certification, disclosure, and verification, because those mechanisms shape whether green bonds can be trusted [N4-F4][N7-R2]. **Market questions** are embedded in studies of pricing, investor behavior, and market efficiency, because they ask how green bonds are valued and traded [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. **Environmental questions** are embedded in studies of emissions, carbon reduction, and ecological outcomes, because they ask whether green bonds actually move the needle on sustainability [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. In other words, empirical green bond research is not neatly divided into separate “market,” “policy,” and “environment” categories; rather, the same study is often read as answering multiple questions simultaneously, with the choice of objective category depending on the dependent variable and the framing of the research question [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R1][N6-R2][N7-R2].

Overall, the literature is strongest on **market outcomes** and **environmental effectiveness**, while **certification/credibility** and **greenwashing** are increasingly important but still relatively narrower in scope [N5-R2][N5-R3][N6-R2][N7-R2][N7-R3]. The main limitation is that the categories are often not mutually exclusive, so a single paper can straddle multiple objectives; this makes it difficult to cleanly separate empirical studies into a single category without losing nuance [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R1][N6-R2][N7-R2].

# How empirical research on green bonds can be systematically categorized according to their primary research objectives

Empirical research on green bonds is best understood as a field that is not neatly partitioned into one objective category per paper, but rather organized around a small number of **overlapping primary objectives**. The literature most commonly treats these categories as **mutually reinforcing** rather than mutually exclusive: studies often ask about **market outcomes**, **environmental impact**, **certification and credibility**, and **greenwashing or credibility gaps** at the same time [N1-F1][N3-F3][N4-F4][N5-R1][N6-R2][N7-R2]. This overlap means that any systematic categorization must recognize that the same paper can belong to more than one objective category, and that these categories are not cleanly separable in empirical design [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R1][N6-R2][N7-R2].

## 1) The main objective categories used in the literature

The empirical literature on green bonds is organized around five main objective categories, with the first four being especially dominant:

### 1.1) **Market and pricing outcomes**
This is one of the most common categories. The literature frequently asks how green bonds are priced, whether they show a “green premium,” and how market participants react to them. Studies in this category examine yield spreads, pricing efficiency, investor sentiment, and market contagion, often comparing green bonds with conventional bonds [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. These studies are often framed as market-based investigations of how investors and traders interpret green bonds, and they are especially common in papers on green bond pricing anomalies and investor behavior [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3].

### 1.2) **Environmental impact and effectiveness**
A second major category is whether green bonds actually improve environmental outcomes. This includes studies of carbon reduction, emissions intensity, ecological footprint, and broader sustainability performance [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. Some papers also examine whether green bond issuance is associated with improved corporate environmental performance, often with a focus on emissions, pollution control, or other environmental metrics [N3-F3][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5]. This category is often the environmental counterpart to the market category: it asks whether the bond delivers real environmental benefits, not just whether investors think it does [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R5].

### 1.3) **Certification and credibility**
A growing but still narrower category is the study of certification, disclosure, and verification. Papers in this category examine how third-party certification affects pricing, market trust, and perceived credibility [N3-F3][N4-F4]. They often ask whether certification actually improves outcomes or whether it merely signals credibility without affecting the real environmental effect [N3-F3][N4-F4]. These studies are especially relevant because certification is central to how investors interpret green bonds, and because verification is increasingly treated as a market prerequisite rather than an optional feature [N4-F4][N4-R4].

### 1.4) **Greenwashing, verification gaps, and credibility mechanisms**
This category is closely related to certification and credibility but is often framed as a **structural limitation** rather than merely a descriptive topic. It asks whether green bonds are genuinely green, whether they reflect opportunistic signaling, and whether verification gaps or credibility gaps exist in the market [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3]. Some studies argue that greenwashing is not widespread but that credibility gaps remain important concerns [N7-R2]. This category is especially important because it addresses the **quality of evidence** underlying the other categories: if certification is weak, the environmental and market effects may be overstated [N3-F3][N4-F4][N7-R2].

### 1.5) **Policy and regulatory design**
While less explicitly emphasized in the provided evidence than the other categories, policy questions are still present in the literature. They arise especially in studies of certification, disclosure, verification, and regional standards, because these mechanisms shape whether green bonds can be trusted and how they are governed [N1-F1][N4-F4][N7-R2]. The evidence also suggests that regional and standard-based frameworks vary, which implies that policy design is an important underlying concern for empirical research [N1-F1][N4-F4].

## 2) Why the same study can belong to more than one category

A major reason the literature is not cleanly divided into a single category per paper is that **research questions often overlap**. For example:

- A paper on whether green bonds improve environmental performance may also be concerned with certification quality, because third-party certification is central to whether the environmental effect is credible [N3-F3][N4-F4].
- A study on investor sentiment or pricing may also touch on disclosure quality or credibility, because investor behavior depends on how investors interpret the greenness and reliability of the bond [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N4-F4].
- A study on greenwashing may also be framed as an issue of market outcomes or investor behavior, because credibility gaps affect how investors price and trade green bonds [N7-R1][N7-R3][N5-R1].

In short, the literature often treats **policy, market, and environmental questions** as interrelated rather than separate. A single empirical paper may be read as answering multiple questions at once: “Is this bond actually green?” “How is it priced?” and “Does it reduce emissions?” [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R1][N6-R2][N7-R2].

## 3) Which categories are most commonly used versus niche

The most commonly used categories are clearly **market outcomes** and **environmental impact**. The market literature is especially rich in studies of yield spreads, pricing anomalies, and investor behavior, including the green premium and pricing efficiency [N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The environmental literature is also substantial, with a focus on carbon reduction, emissions intensity, and ecological outcomes [N6-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4][N6-R5].

In contrast, **certification/credibility** and **greenwashing/credibility gaps** are increasingly important but still relatively narrower in scope. These categories are central to studies of third-party verification, greenwashing, and credibility mechanisms, but they are often framed as addressing gaps rather than as the dominant empirical focus [N3-F3][N4-F4][N7-R2][N7-R3]. **Policy and regulatory design** is present in the literature but thinner in the provided evidence than the other categories, especially compared to market and environmental research [N1-F1][N4-F4].

### Policy questions
These are embedded in studies of certification, disclosure, verification, and regional standards. They ask whether the green bond market is trustworthy, whether verification is effective, and how different frameworks affect governance [N1-F1][N4-F4][N7-R2]. The evidence suggests that verification and certification are not merely background features; they shape the entire empirical design and interpretation [N3-F3][N4-F4].

The evidence also shows that credibility mechanisms can change market outcomes directly, because investors may accept lower yields in exchange for environmental alignment [N3-F3][N5-R2].
